newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM rules out "administrative" trade moves.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM rules out "administrative" trade moves.

text.p: Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Tuesday that the Czech Republic's large trade deficit was to be expected and his government planned no direct administrative measures to counter it.

Speaking to a banking conference, he said the trade gap -- which led to a 1996 current account deficit of roughly nine percent of gross domestic product and showed no signs of improvement this year -- was "normal".
"There is no easy way how to change it. We can easily imagine the use of some administrative restrictions, but this is not what we intend to do in this country," Klaus said.
The government has repeatedly ruled out a devaluation of the crown to boost exports, and has also rejected the imposition of any import surcharges as well.

Klaus however again took issue with the Czech National Bank's monetary policy and its effect on economic growth, but he played down concerns about a slight downturn in the economy, from 4.8 percent real growth in 1995 to 4.4 percent in 1996.
"I think the debate is a little bit overdone and overplayed," he said.

Analysts however point out that official forecasts had projected 1996 growth at over five percent, and many say that real growth of seven or eight percent was necessary to quickly narrow the gap with neighbouring countries in the European Union which the Czechs are eager to join.
Klaus said the government was waiting on early 1997 data "so that we can seriously debate what the trend is".

He said that with the central bank's tightening measures last June -- when it raised its key discount rate one full percentage point to 10.5 percent and increased commercial banks' minimum reserve requirements -- "monetary policy went from a passive policy to an active one".
"I have to say that our central bankers have dreamt of such a possibility for a long time."

The central bank tightened monetary policy to stem a surge in domestic demand which had been keeping inflation above nine percent in the first half last year. By February, inflation had slowed to 7.3 percent, year-on-year.
Klaus said because of the tightening moves, growth slowed and the external trade imbalance "probably even deepened."
"The impact... on aggregrate supply was even stronger in the shortrun than the impact on aggregate demand," Klaus said
